Review:
Naughty Nuri’s has been my all-time favorite since 2015, and honestly, it has never changed — in the best way possible. Every visit feels like coming back to an old friend. The flavors are always consistent, bold, and absolutely delicious. From the first bite to the last, the food is just as yummy as I remember years ago. What I truly appreciate is how they’ve managed to maintain the same quality and taste over time. No shortcuts, no disappointment — just solid, satisfying food every single time. On top of that, the staff are always friendly, welcoming, and attentive, which makes the whole experience even better. You can really feel the warm, relaxed vibe that Naughty Nuri’s is known for. It’s rare to find a place that stays this good for so many years, but Naughty Nuri’s does it effortlessly. If you’re looking for a place that’s reliable, flavorful, and full of good energy, this is it. Will always keep coming back. Highly recommended! 👌🔥

Review:
Amazing joint from the original one in Ubud. This place ticked all the boxes for me but with an upgrade on the environment from the original. Think modern sleek woodwork still reminiscent of Bali but in a Texan-Saloon setting. Pictures of old cartoon, paraphernalia & records hung on the walls. A semi-open kitchen gives you a peering insight into the wonders of the flaming grill. A large pot of the signature sauce next to it while the chefs lathers on the sticky-sweet-savoury liquid onto the ribs. The grilled prawns as a starter were an absolute gem. Succulent, plump & sweet (not to mentioned well cleaned which is a big plus). The garlic butter brushed on had the right twang to it and made it even more moorish. Then came the main star. A half rack of ribs weighing in at 600g (bone-in). The steaming aroma was hard to miss and a quick squeeze of lime made my mouth salivate. Even now writing this makes me crave it despite having dinner already. The bones fall apart and the meat just melts over. Sticky, gnarly and downright dirty, this isn’t a first-date meal but boy does it make for one heck of a dinner. Washed it down with their homemade ice tea to cool the palate. I skipped the sides to keep space for the ribs but the patrons around who had them seemed to enjoy it. Do come by & try it when in Seminyak!

Review:
I had the chance to visit Warung Babi Guling Pande Egi in Gianyar, Bali, and it was an unforgettable experience. Tucked away on the way from main road to Ubud this warung is a gem surrounded by lush rice fields, offering a serene backdrop that instantly sets a relaxed vibe. The open-air dining area is spacious, clean, and modern yet retains a traditional Balinese charm—perfect for soaking in the cool breeze while enjoying a meal. I arrived around 11.30 am, and the place was buzzing with locals and tourists alike, a testament to its popularity. Despite the crowd, the staff was incredibly efficient, using electric buzzers to manage the waitlist, which kept things organized. I was seated almost immediately with a stunning view of the rice paddies. I ordered the **Nasi Babi Guling Jumbo** (IDR 38,000, roughly $2.50 USD), which came loaded with tender suckling pig, crispy pork skin, pork sausage, lawar (a traditional Balinese vegetable mix), pork satay, and a savory pork soup. The pork was melt-in-your-mouth soft, with a smoky, well-spiced flavor, and the skin was perfectly crackly. The sambal matah added a fresh, spicy kick that tied everything together. I also tried their “es daluman”, a refreshing dessert beverage of mixed grass jelly in coconut milk and palm sugar, which was a great palate cleanser. The service was friendly and professional, even with the hectic pace. The warung has clearly evolved since its early days as a small local spot in 2016, now boasting a larger space and extras like coffee and Balinese “jajanan pasar” (local cakes and desserts). I noticed a group next to me order a whole roasted pig for takeout, which looked impressive and apparently feeds 6-12 people for around $120 AUD. My only minor gripe was the wait time during busy hours (noon), but the food and ambiance made it worthwhile. If you’re planning a visit, I’d recommend arriving early (before noon) to beat the rush or catching the sunset for an even more picturesque experience. Warung Babi Guling Pande Egi lives up to its legendary status as one of Bali’s best babi guling spots—highly recommended for anyone craving authentic Balinese cuisine in a beautiful settings and local price! Worthy note: Pande in Balinese = craftsmen Him/his family line previously probably metal craftsmen

I visited this place with a friend on a Friday morning around 10am for breakfast. We didn't have a reservation and were told there would be at least a 20-minute wait, but could sit in the waiting area. That area is unfortunately right next to a construction site in the back, which wasn't very comfortable. After about 10 minutes we were seated and asked if we were okay sharing a table with other guests. While I generally don't mind shared tables, we ended up at a large table shared by several different parties. Combined with how busy, loud, and crowded the space already was, it felt quite overwhelming and had a bit of an assembly-line atmosphere. The café itself is nicely designed in a rustic, wooden style, but due to how packed it was, the overall vibe felt stressful rather than cozy. Conversation was difficult because of the noise level. Service felt rather slow. The coffee was genuinely good, and the banana bread was fine, but nothing particularly memorable. I've had noticeably better breakfast and coffee in Canggu, Pererenan, and the surrounding area over the last years. While I appreciate that the staff asked before seating us at a shared table, and it ultimately was our choice, the combination of crowding, noise, and hype took away from the experience. For me, this isn't a place I'd return to for a relaxed breakfast.

I went here for dinner to try their Indonesian dishes and left quite impressed. The oxtail soup from the main menu was rich, aromatic, and deeply comforting, with meat so tender it easily fell off the bone. The broth had a beautiful balance of warmth and spice, complemented by the chili and sweet soy sauce served on the side. The dish came with rice and emping (melinjo chips), which rounded out the flavours perfectly. The second dish, featured on a seasonal menu, was grilled octopus with finely chopped snake beans stir-fried in Balinese spices. The combination of the tender octopus and the crunchy, aromatic snake beans made this dish memorable and full of texture. I also appreciated the staff’s clarity when explaining that “Draft Beer” referred to a local brand rather than a traditional keg pour. Hence, a classic Bintang was ordered instead. Overall, the experience was satisfying, with attentive service and well-balanced local flavours worth revisiting.

Review:
WHO GAVE THESE PEOPLE THE RIGHT TO BE THIS GOOD? I’ve been to Pison Ubud twice now, and let me tell you, it’s so consistently excellent it’s starting to annoy me. Nobody should be this good at feeding people unless they’re trying to overthrow a government. You walk in and the place is vibing, all style, energy, and good-looking people pretending they’re not checking their reflections in every shiny surface. The staff? Exceptional. Too exceptional. Smiling, attentive, helpful like they’re auditioning to be adopted into your family. I’m suspicious of that level of kindness; it usually means someone’s stealing your watch. But no, they’re just… good. It’s unsettling. Now let’s talk food. I had the Seafood Spaghetti, and dear God, it was so scrumptious I nearly applauded. That’s embarrassing. No grown adult should clap for pasta unless they’re at an intervention. Perfectly cooked, flavours bursting, the kind of dish that makes you rethink your life choices, like, ‘Why don’t I live here? Why do I bother cooking at home like a fool?’ Then the Truffle Tenderloin Steak; juicy, gorgeous, covered in truffle like it’s trying to seduce you. I've eaten steak in a lot of places, sweetheart, and half of them should be in prison compared to this. This thing melted in my mouth so gracefully I filed a police report for emotional manipulation. Pison is the kind of place that’s so good, so polished, so utterly on point that you leave feeling slightly inferior. You want to improve yourself just so you deserve their dessert. So here’s the truth: Food: Outrageous. Stop showing off. Service: Kind enough to make you suspicious. Atmosphere: Cool people pretending not to stare at your shirt. Overall: If you go to Ubud and miss this place, you’re the kind of person who goes to Paris and eats at the airport. Pison Ubud, I love you. I hate how much I love you. I’ll be back. And I’ll insult you again. That’s how affection works, sweetheart.

Review:
We came here to celebrate my father-in-law's 60th birthday with the whole family. We were ushered upstairs to a very nice private space that could sit 10-15 people. The whole atmosphere was pleasant and suprisingly kid friendly as we had a total of 4 children. We had the fine dining set order by candlelights. Our server was Rudy and his team, they were very welcoming, fun, and hospitable. Food wise, we started off with Mahi Mahi with potato bread. This for me was probably the best combination of bread and dipping sauce. The Mahi Mahi was marvelous, very creamy with that hint of fishy taste at every bite. It was a wholesome experience. Then came the tuna tartelette and jamom croquette. The tartelette was zingy and flavourful as a mouthful, I personally liked that. The croquette was creamy and blended perfectly with the saltiness of the jamon. As for the ceviche, it was alright though, my famumily had the same sentiments. We probably expected it to be a bit more sour and vinegarey, but this one somehow lacked a bit of those elements for our liking, some even commented it tasting a little sweet. Now for the shared mains, we had dry aged grouper, lamb shoulder, and potato mille. Not many of us appreciated the grouper, although it was presented well and had that crispy skin, we found the meat a tad bit mushy in some parts. The lamb was a delight though, very soft, almost a melt-in-your-mouth kind of attempt. It tasted a little gamey, but we all were used which we didn't mind at all. On that note, most of us wished it was a potato mash instead of mille. We thought it would've been a more rounded pairing with the lamb. But the mille was crunchy and soft inside, we all liked it. Finally, as a dessert person, my winner would probably be the churros. It had that perfect crunch and soft core. The dulce de leche was a nice touch as it melts the chocolate on top of the churros. The amalgamation of all the components in this dessert was very well executed. It was a delightful experience altogether. The staff also prepared a candle for my father-in-law to blow, and they catered very well to the children. Our team of servers were very fun and accommodating. This definitely made our whole experience a comfortable and memorable one. The restaurant should be proud of their staff, very kind and go above and beyond. We highly recommend this restaurant if you want to try a fine-dining experience with its own flair and genuine service!

Review:
Bali was our third port stop on a 28 day Asia cruise and we were lucky to have an overnight stay here. On our first day we hired a private tour guide through a tour company but sadly he wasn’t willing to take us where we wanted to go. I had hoped to bring my little daughters to the beach but after over four hours of driving he brought us to a beach restaurant in the dark. Disappointed we canceled our second day with that company and decided to take a chance with a driver from the port. That’s how we met Kadek Agus, an older gentleman who was incredibly kind, patient and sincere. I told him how much I had wanted to try Bali’s famous suckling pig, something I’d seen on Mark Wiens’ food videos. I had mentioned this to our guide the day before while we were in Ubud but perhaps because he was Muslim he steered us away and said it was too far or not available. I had tucked that food wish away thinking it just wasn’t going to happen. When I told Kadek Agus about it he said with such honesty that yes the suckling pig was indeed in Ubud, where we had just been yesterday, and now it was too far since the ship was leaving later that day. I was disappointed but I really appreciated his transparency and effort. He took us to another place that served pork but unfortunately the satay was too spicy for my little girls and they weren’t able to adjust it. As we were driving again I spotted Wahaha Pork Ribs in Jimbaran and asked if we could stop. It ended up being the perfect decision. While I had hoped for more traditional Balinese food sometimes moms have to adjust and this was just what our family needed. The staff were incredibly welcoming. When they saw my daughters getting bitten by mosquitoes the hostess kindly offered us bug spray to keep them comfortable. Service was fast helpful and kind throughout. We ordered the pork ribs for the kids and the pork knuckle for ourselves. The knuckle was huge and carved tableside, crispy juicy and hands down the best pork knuckle I’ve ever had. My husband was happy to discover they were offering a buy one get one free caipirinha special which was a fun bonus. Wahaha really delivered on flavor service and comfort. It turned out to be a highlight of our Bali stop and we’re so grateful to Kadek Agus for his thoughtfulness and care. Highly recommend both the restaurant and this wonderful driver if you ever find yourself arriving by cruise in Bali.

Malini Uluwatu is all about the view — and yes, the view is absolutely stunning. The restaurant sits right on the cliff, and the seaside scenery is truly beautiful and dramatic. Unfortunately, that’s where the positives mostly end. We reserved a table in advance, which is the only reason we got a direct seaside view. On top of that, there are very few vegetarian options — basically none. If you don’t eat seafood or meat, your choices are extremely limited. The seating is uncomfortable: • Hard, uncomfortable chairs • Very little space — your knees are literally against the wall • Not a place to sit and enjoy a relaxed meal Overall, Malini is only worth visiting for the view. The food is bland and uninspired, the portions are far too small, and the comfort level is low. If you’re looking for a special table (anniversary, engagement, birthday, etc.), you need to very clearly and repeatedly communicate this in advance — and even then, there’s no guarantee you’ll get it. Personally, I would not recommend this restaurant unless you’re only coming for the scenery and photos. For good food, comfort, and value, there are much better options in Uluwatu.

Review:
This Padang styled restaurant is a must try for all visitors to Jakarta. In fact, there are a few outlets carrying the Pagi Sore brand, but we specially decided to choose this particular one, on our way to the airport, before we fly back to KL. Najwa had been mentioning the name ever since day 1, but our itinerary had been quite packed throughout our soujourn in Jakarta. Hence, it was such a great opportunity to be able to try it on our very last day. We have tried plenty of Nasi Padang restaurants before, the Simpang Tiga restaurants in Medan and Ipoh, as well as the various Rumah Sederhana outlets in Malaysia. But Pagi Sore is distinctly unique. Upon our arrival, we were quickly ushered to our Table for 4, and as we were sitting down, some foods were also being continuously piled up on our table. I know that we would be charged only for those we actually ate, but the delectable spread being presented in front of our eyes were very hard to resist!! So, some ground rules needed to be established to ensure we didnt encourage any wastages. This was a major challenge for Daniel, ad he was so used to finishing all the leftovers!! I just couldnt resist the huge Fresh Water Prawn which was staring directly at my face, and decided to do justice to it. My wife and Najwa loved the Ayam Bumbu Putih, the Chicken with White Gravy, and I also found that dish to be marvelously delicious too. Daniel and I ended up finishing a plate of what looked like some crackers, which actually turned out to be Keropok Kulit Sapi, or Cow's Hide crackers...go figure.. All in all, it was such a fullfilling lunch, and Najwa settled the bills with a big smile, as the cost was very agreable to her. Obviously, I would happily recommend this restaurant to others..

restaurant: RM Pagi Sore PIK (Resto & PS Coffee)

Phoenix Rising (and Ordering Tequila) A neurotic love letter to steak, staircases, and traffic gods in Jakarta. You don’t go to Phoenix Gastrobar — you embark on a pilgrimage. If the traffic gods smile upon you (which they rarely do, those vindictive bastards), it’s a one-hour drive from Jakarta proper. If they don’t, it’s a two-act opera about mortality set inside a Grab. But when you finally arrive, sweaty, hopeful, and spiritually tested, the place hits you like a mirage designed by Hogwarts’ architect after a night out with Willy Wonka. There are stairwells that cross each other like a M.C. Escher drawing that gave up trying to be logical, secret passages that make you question reality, and lights so warm and moody you start narrating your own life like a noir film. I half-expected Dumbledore to walk past with a martini. The food? Exceptional. Capital E exceptional. The steak — divine. Charred outside, tender inside, like it had been serenaded by angels with tongs. The service is impeccable in that polite, silent way that says, “We know it’s expensive, but we also know you’ll forgive us.” And you do. Because the moment you taste that first bite, you realise this isn’t just dinner — it’s repentance for every bad meal you’ve ever endured. Yes, it’s expensive by Indonesian standards. But so is happiness, and this place delivers both on a plate. When you’re done, stroll (or stagger) next door to Tiger Club, the kind of place where the lighting is forgiving and the tequila is not. Order recklessly, stay irresponsibly late, and watch as night dissolves into day — because that’s what happens when you mix good steak, great music, and a small existential crisis over the bill. Phoenix Gastrobar isn’t just a restaurant. It’s a fever dream with cutlery. Go. Bring friends. Bring a map. Bring a sense of wonder. And pray to the traffic gods on your way back — they might just grant you mercy.

Review:
IT SHOULD TASTE LIKE PENANG. NOT KL. I came to Hameediyah with my friend and my mother, expecting the comfort of a good plate of nasi kandar. Instead, what I got was an experience that felt half-show, half-food — and only slightly satisfying. The queue was long, as expected — but that’s not the problem. What really threw me off was the behaviour of certain people in the line. There were customers more focused on filming themselves than ordering their food. Loud TikTok narrations. Tripods set up in the middle of walkways. People posing with plates while others waited patiently behind them. It was disrespectful, disruptive, and honestly, exhausting. If you came here for makan, you had to push past a content-creator circus just to get to the counter. When it was finally my turn, I stood in front of a wide range of lauk, trying to decide. Classic kuah campur for me — I like the chaos, the flavour, the mess. The prawns caught my eye — fat, glossy, drowning in orange curry — but I hesitated. Pricey, intimidating, and I didn’t want to be disappointed. So I passed. Taste-wise, Hameediyah sits in a strange space — somewhere between KL’s polished, curated tourist scene and Penang’s unapologetic bare minimum. It tries to hold onto heritage, but feels semi-delivered. Safe. Predictable. Sanitised, even. Then came my mother. No chaos, no confusion. She stood at the counter and said clearly: “Kari kambing. Sayur. Jangan campur.” No extra instructions. No need for the gravy drama. Even the abang hesitated — like her request went against some kind of nasi kandar rulebook. But she didn’t flinch. Her plate was focused, grounded, and quietly bold. It reminded me that sometimes, less truly is more. We also shared a murtabak, which unfortunately, was the low point of the visit. Murtabak should be judged by how generous it is with filling, how thick it folds, how the meat spills at the edge. Hameediyah’s wasn’t a textbook — it was a primary school exercise book. Thin, underfilled, dry. Definitely not worth the price tag. I’ve had better from pasar Ramadan stalls under plastic tents, wrapped in oily brown paper. To me, a good nasi kandar should haunt you after the meal. It should cling to your fingers with spice, leave your shirt faintly smelling of curry, and stay with you for hours — in all the best ways. But Hameediyah didn’t do that. It felt… semi-delivered. Like someone had wrapped up a memory and served it reheated. Come here if you want to say you’ve been. Take your photos, maybe even enjoy a decent plate. But if you’re looking for that true, finger-staining, gravy-sticking-to-your-spoon experience — the one that tastes like a messy plate at 11am in Penang or Butterworth — you’ll need to keep looking.

Their signature Ipoh-style short and thick bean sprouts are fresh, crunchy, and lightly stir-fried. It’s also impressively clean for this style of restaurant- no slippery floors or greasy kitchen surfaces. Plus, the back kitchen even has a view of some back alley wall art! Definitely coming back.

A Disappointing Experience at Onn Kee Chicken Rice. I'm usually not one to write negative reviews, but my recent experience at Onn Kee Chicken Rice was a letdown, to say the least. My family visited this popular eatery, expecting a delicious and satisfying meal. Unfortunately, our expectations were not met. We ordered the 3-portion chicken for the three of us, but the servings were surprisingly small. There was hardly any meat on the bone, and we were left feeling unsatisfied. For a stall that's supposed to the specialty of Ipoh well known and specialize in chicken rice, you'd expect the chilli sauce to be a highlight, but unfortunately, it was a disappointment. To be honest, I've had better chicken rice in Singapore, and I wouldn't recommend Onn Kee to anyone looking for a delicious and satisfying meal. Unless they seriously revamp their recipe and improve their service, I'd advise eating at Onn Kee at your own risk. Honestly, hiring foreigners has affected the image. To make matters worse, living in its yester years of past glory, sooner and not later, you will see the name become a past history. Rating: 2/5 stars Will I return? Unlikely.

Review:
Visited Ipoh Tuck Kee Restaurant during dinner time, and it was easy to understand why this place is always packed with customers. Despite arriving around 5:45pm, the restaurant was already full, and a queue had formed outside. Luckily, the waiting time wasn’t too long as the staff manage the crowd efficiently. The staff here are friendly, attentive, and extremely fast. They move with purpose, clearing tables quickly, taking orders proactively, and ensuring customers are seated as soon as possible. Even with the high customer volume, they remain polite and alert, which makes the whole experience smooth and pleasant. The environment is typical of a popular local eatery — crowded, lively, and full of energy. Even though it gets busy, it remains comfortable and organized. Tables are fairly close to each other, but the quick turnover ensures that the place doesn’t feel stuffy. In terms of price, it’s reasonable for the portion sizes and the quality of food served. The food portion matches the pricing well, with ingredients that feel fresh and dishes that are cooked with consistency. Now, onto the highlight — the braised chicken leg. This dish is truly outstanding and highly recommended. The chicken leg is tender, juicy, and packed with flavour. The braising sauce is rich and savory, absorbing beautifully into the meat. It’s one of those dishes that instantly stands out and becomes a must-order for future visits. The other dishes we tried were also good, maintaining the flavorful and satisfying taste that Tuck Kee is known for. Overall, Ipoh Tuck Kee Restaurant lives up to its reputation as one of Ipoh’s top spots for delicious local dishes. The long queue might seem intimidating, but with the fast service and efficient turnover, the wait is very manageable. If you’re visiting Ipoh and looking for a dinner place that balances taste, value, and local charm, Tuck Kee is definitely worth a stop.

Review:
One of Bukit Mertajam's Michelin award eateries, this place has been drawing crowds locally and outstation. It is located along Jalan Betek in an unassuming location, which looks more like a car respray workshop. This also means that when the eatery opens at 6pm, there is some space for parking. We were fortunate to arrive when the crowd has not built yet on a Wednesday evening. Ordered two plates of regular char koay teow with duck eggs, which came to RM9 (at the time of writing). The dishes came relatively quickly. The char koay teow does not look much like the typical Penang char koay teow as it is darker and not as spicy (even though we mentioned that we are OK with chilli). Visually, it does not look appetising, but surprisingly it tasted really good. It had lots of wok hei, presumably from the use of charcoal fire, and the pork lard pieces were crispy and delicious. The eggs were perfectly cooked and the runny egg yolk added a different layer of umami compared to normal char koay teow. Portions were also adequate and we left feeling satisfied. You also have the option of adding side dishes, though we chose not to do so. A nice place to eat and will return as long as prices are maintained.

Output:
restaurant: Ming Qin Charchol Duck Egg Char Koay Teow

The sauce is salty and addictive to complement the tender octopus. It doesn’t matter which part you eat, they are all tender, not rubbery or chewy. The head of the octopus, kind of satisfyingly pops when chewed. The chilli sauce that accompanies it is delicious and enhances the taste a little bit to the already delicious dish. Overall it’s a good meal to try for these two dishes. A single toilet is available at the end of the air conditioned room. For these 2 dishes, octopus rm28 and Ckt rm10.

On my mom's phone like usual to make a review since she's not the kind of person who makes reviews. But anyways, we went to BM Yam Rice Kopitiam on our last day (which was the day we were going to go home) in Penang, 7 October which was yesterday for lunch. Ordered the signature yam rice with pork soup (there were two bowls of pork soup, one with what i think is what usually is, pork belly, a type of pork cut i don't know and meatballs.)The other bowl had some weirder cuts (that i don't like but my parents love) think there was pork intestine but i forgot the pork cuts/parts of the rest in that soup. The pork itself in the soup tasted great too. And the pork soup was a great combo with the yam rice. The yam rice was a little salty but it was really good, i don't quite know how to describe the taste but i really liked it, especially paired with the pork soup. Oh yeah, we also ordered the braised tofu and egg which were good too. I had specially drank some of the soup and ate some of the pork and a little of my yam rice before picking some pork (and a meatball) and a half braised egg and placed them in my yam rice before chopping the egg with my spoon and mixing the yam rice with it and with the pork and meatball too (it tasted great!) I don't know how much it costed since my parents were the one that paid and they forgot how much it was. But anyways, i'd say this place was a pretty solid 4/5 out of 5 stars, though i put it four stars since i only went there once (oh and that time was also my first time eating yam rice, so yam rice had a pretty good first impression on me from this place) Anyways, i would recommend this place to people going to Penang and haven't decided what to eat yet (and especially if they haven't eaten yam rice before or like yam rice) And yep, that's all, it's a little long but oh well, overall, it was a great experience (and as usual, i was the last one to finish my bowl, since i like doing everything and maybe especially eating at my own pace)

I've been coming to this yam rice shop since I was young, and I am truly happy that they got recognized by Michelin. They absolutely deserve it. Some people might say they've had better yam rice elsewhere, or that this place is overrated, and that's okay – everyone has their opinion. But in my mind, this is the hands-down best. They also offer some side dishes like braised tofu and egg in dark sauce, and braised pork knuckles. Don't expect fancy decor. The place is old-school and hasn't changed a bit since they moved to this premise. You come here for the amazing, affordable food, and that's it. With their delicious dishes and reasonable prices, anyone visiting Bukit Mertajam should definitely check them out.

Review:
This is the Japanese restaurant that went viral online for its huge tonkatsu, and it truly lived up to the hype. The tonkatsu portions were extremely big and very well cooked. I also really liked their miso soup and Japanese rice, which were surprisingly good. It was my first time having miso soup filled with so much chicken meat and vegetables, instead of the usual small amount of seaweed and tiny tofu found at most restaurants. Their opening time was 6pm. We arrived at 5.30pm on a Saturday, but there was already a long queue waiting outside. The restaurant only has around 16–17 seats, and unfortunately, my friend and I were the 18th in line, so we had to wait for the second round. Luckily, the staff took down everyone’s name on a waiting list, so we didn’t have to stand there the whole time. We finally got our seats after about 1 hour. The staff patiently explained the differences between the various pork cuts, and we could watch the chef cooking right in front of us. We ordered the fatty Sakura pork set and the lean premium pork set, and later added an à la carte small muscle katsu. The set came with refillable rice, cabbage, and miso soup. Out of the three types of katsu we tried, the muscle katsu was my favourite. It had a springier texture and stronger flavour compared to the others. The Sakura pork had a layer of fat that gave a unique texture and taste, but the meat itself was slightly tougher. The premium pork was somewhere in between, and honestly, I couldn’t really tell what made it “premium,” even though it was the thickest cut. That said, it was still cooked nicely with a slight pinkness in the middle. The best part of all was the light and crispy crust, which was not oily at all. Even after eating so much fried food, we didn’t feel heavy or jelak at all.

Review:
Came here with friends during lunch for Omakase without reservation. The staff was graciously welcoming us in. Luckily it wasn't fully occupied, hence we were given the bar seat. Since it was my first Omakase experience, hence I have no comparison to draw with unlike my other 2 friends. They were certainly impressed and wowed away by the food prepared by the chef. As for me, as I was recovering from COVID and in midst of regaining my sense of smell and taste, I guess I do enjoy some of the stronger tasting dishes, and especially the texture of the food. I liked the attention paid to the details on the combination of the food, the sequences of having them in order to fully savour the textures and flavours of each ingredients the chef has prepared. Even their cutleries are fascinating and cute. Again, I would say I'm giving 4 🌟 even though I couldn't taste all food but because of the atmosphere, customer service, food presentation and the chef's skills while preparing our Omakase. I underestimated their food portion, thinking I would still be hungry after the course meal, which was NOT true. We were full and satiated(so much for our back-up plan to head to Edo-Ichi/Daorae across the street thereafter). Well worth the meal indeed. Will definitely return again to fully enjoy the taste the next time I get my taste and smell back. Side note: Better to make reservations for bar counter to watch all the action. Their selection of sake is delightful, also they allow you to choose a sake cup design you like.

Music choices enhanced this effect with the old school songs playing in the background too! Such attention to detail! Well done to the cook, and the team for the food and service too! Restaurant Titi Papan in Bukit Mertajam is hands down one of the best spots to enjoy a rich, flavorful curry meal. The dishes are always served warm and fresh, and if by chance it’s not hot enough, you can just request them to reheat it on the spot. In the mornings, their roti canai and chapati are top picks for breakfast—soft, fluffy, and perfect with their thick dhal or curry. Review:
Song Fa Bak Kut Teh at New Bridge Road is one of those places I keep coming back to, and it never disappoints. This particular outlet is my favorite. It sits on a corner shophouse, open and airy, with a very comfortable feel even when it is busy. I have never dined at their other branches because this one already feels just right for me. The atmosphere here is simple and welcoming. Natural airflow, high ceilings, and the classic shophouse charm make the whole meal more enjoyable. It feels relaxed and unpretentious, exactly how bak kut teh should be enjoyed. The star of the show is, of course, the bak kut teh. The peppery broth is bold, aromatic, and deeply satisfying. Every sip warms you up and keeps you reaching for more. The pork is tender and cooked just right, soaking up all that beautiful peppery goodness. It is the kind of dish that tastes consistent every single time, which is why I always enjoy eating here. The sides deserve special mention. Honestly, do not skip them. The sides here elevate the whole experience. From the ones I ordered, they are easily some of the best sides you can pair with bak kut teh. Each dish complements the soup perfectly and adds variety to the meal. I really recommend ordering the sides generously, as they make the table feel complete. Apologies for my photos, as a few side dishes were missing when I took them. We also had the braised pork samchan and intestines served on one plate, which were rich, flavorful, and very well done. There was also the trio of boiled peanuts and tofu, plus one more item on the same plate that slipped my mind, all comforting and nicely seasoned. And of course, the dough fritters are a must. Dipping them into the hot soup is one of the best parts of the meal. Song Fa Bak Kut Teh at New Bridge Road remains my go-to spot for bak kut teh in Singapore. Great food, a comfortable setting, and consistently satisfying flavors. This is one of those places I will always return to without hesitation. Highly recommended.

Output:
restaurant: Song Fa Bak Kut Teh 11 New Bridge Road

A super famous Bak Kut Teh (a.k.a. meat bone tea) franchise in the heart of Singapore city center! This is the one place that opens up one hour early at 10am, whereas the rest of the locations open at 11am! It was packed from the beginning when we got there at 10:08 AM, and we got lucky, and got the last table open after it opened! We ordered a few bone soups, braised pork, and vegetable dish (refer to the receipt), and they were all quite good as expected. The food wasn't heavy, the portion wasn't to overwhelming, and it was one of the cheapest meals we had in Singapore as well! The soup wasn't too heavy or oily, and it was soothing to the stomach. The soup itself was also refillable for free! One negative I have to say is that it seemed to have too much pepper. I actually found the bak kut teh I had in Rasapura Masters food court better tasting than here! Everything was very efficient, ordering online through QR code, and they serve you right away. The staff was friendly and attentive even though it was really busy. By the time we got out (in 40 minutes or so), there was a huge line up outside. However, because there are many tables, and the rotation is quite fast, so you probably won't have to wait too much in the line. I would strongly recommend to go to this place right when it opens, and for only a group of 4 or less.

Review:
If you’re chasing the ultimate plate of fried kway teow in Singapore, this legendary stall at Hong Lim Market & Food Centre is my top pick. Every visit feels like a reunion with comfort food done right. The “wok hei” here is unmistakable—smoky, intense, and deeply satisfying. And that signature pork lard smile? Occasionally, a younger assistant takes over when the uncle’s on break. While the finesse may vary slightly, the taste still holds up well and is worth trying. Be prepared to wait, especially during lunch rush. But honestly? The queue is part of the experience. It builds the anticipation—and the reward is always worth it. This stall consistently satisfies my cravings. It’s a stall that respects tradition, delivers bold flavors, and never compromises on quality. Whether you’re a local or just visiting, this is one plate you shouldn’t miss.

Segar@Chinatown – A Second Date with Zi-Char Comfort Second round at Segar@Chinatown Point and it didn’t disappoint. Nestled on Basement 2, this Halal zi-char spot remains a go-to for good portions, wallet-friendly prices, and consistently hearty flavours. Review:
I’ve been visiting Segar since I was a child, long before they moved from Bedok, even before the construction of Bedok Mall. It’s always been a family favourite, with their claypot golden chicken being a standout dish we’ve loved for years. Recently, we visited their Chinatown Point location. After the original Bedok spot closed, this became our go-to for awhile before the West Coz Cafe was built, but I’m sad to say the quality of the Chinatown outlet has noticeably declined. While the food is still decent and better than many other halal options, it doesn’t quite match the high standard it once did. For instance, the beef fried rice, which used to have a wonderful char and tender beef with crispy rice bits, now lacks that signature char. It’s still flavourful but missing that crispy edge that made it so special. The claypot golden chicken, once a highlight, was also disappointing this time. The golden sauce, usually thick and sticky, was more runny, and the chicken pieces were tough and mostly boney. The sizzling effect and caramelised onions that used to be a treat were missing, and the dish wasn’t served hot enough. On a positive note, the Nonya lady’s finger dish was excellent and maintained its quality. However, the pandan chicken was bland, lacking the aromatic pandan flavour, and the oat prawns, though buttery and sweet, were overcooked and dry. If you’re near HarbourFront, I’d recommend trying the West Coz Cafe location, which offers a taste closer to the original Segar experience. Overall, despite my critique, the food is still bloody good—just not quite up to the exceptional standard I remember from the old days. If you’re near HarbourFront, I’d recommend trying the West Coz Cafe location, which offers a taste closer to the original Segar experience. Unfortunately, the Chinatown Point branch didn’t quite meet expectations, so you might want to consider other options for an authentic Segar meal.

Review:

I ate here at least 2-3x per week for lunch, plus the occasional supper, when there was overtime work to be done. This week I'm visiting 30 years later, it's now called Maxwell Food Centre and the whole area around it is completely different: new skyscrapers all around and an MRT station built in 2022. The 2001 renovation that changed it from a medium sized shed into +3,300 msq facility with more than 100 stalls, apparently cost SGD3.2M! I'm very pleased to say the food stalls are still excellent quality, I had my fill of old favourites: black carrot cake, fried kway teow, and Hianese chicken rice. If you're here for Tian Tian Hianese Chicken Rice with Michelin Bib Gourmand rating, it's better to come early rather than late. There's always a long queue at the stall, and they tend to run out of items late afternoon. When I came on Sunday at 18:00 there was none left of the lovely rice cooked in chicken broth or the roast chicken. So I was able to get steamed chicken only, served cold with warm brown sauce (the only downside of this visit).

Review:
We finally got to try the famous Kok Sen Restaurant, a spot that's always packed and comes with a Michelin Bib Gourmand reputation. Overall, we had a very good and satisfying meal, with every dish being well-executed. It's definitely a top-tier zi char experience, though perhaps the Michelin hype set our expectations a little too high. We ordered a wide spread, including their famous signature dishes. The Big Prawns Hor Fun was a clear standout, with a generous, silky, and flavourful egg gravy that was full of wok hei. The prawns were large and fresh. The Claypot Yong Tau Foo was also excellent; the stuffed items (eggplant, tofu, peppers) were delicious, and the rich, savoury claypot sauce was perfect over rice. The other dishes were all classic and cooked to a high standard. The Crispy Roasted Chicken had paper-thin, crispy skin, and the Stir-fried Beef Hor Fun was loaded with tender beef. We also enjoyed the Prawn Rolls (Hei Zho) and a fluffy Fu Yong Omelette. The service was exactly what you'd expect from a place that is perpetually this busy. It was highly efficient and fast-paced. The star of the dish was undoubtedly the satay sauce, which perfectly complemented the noodles. The rich and creamy satay sauce had just the right balance of sweetness and spiciness, creating a harmonious flavor explosion, which I find it very creative. The noodles, accompanied by tender squid, succulent pork liver, and thinly sliced pork meat, were a delightful addition. The variety of textures and flavors added depth to each bite, making it a truly memorable experience. One word of advice to fellow food enthusiasts: devour this dish quickly! The noodles have a tendency to soak up the flavors, and while that might sound tempting, it's best enjoyed when the noodles are still slightly firm. •Fried Oyster Out of so many dishes the stall offered, I would recommend their Fried Oyster, non-greasy, and the oyster was just cooked right. Little do you know: The difference between fried carrot cake black or white are not only the colour of the sauce itself, but also the taste. To all tourist, remember to choose the white instead as that's what local Singaporean will choose. If you are curious with the black sauce, it tends to be sweeter if you like it.

Review:
Review of Old Airport Road Food Centre Overall, Old Airport Road Food Centre exceeded my expectations with its impressive variety of Singapore heritage dishes. It’s an excellent place to experience a wide range of local flavours, and I’ll continue exploring more stalls and updating this review over time. I also appreciated the creativity behind many stall names, with references to places like Chong Pang, Kallang, and Blanco Court, which add a nostalgic local charm to the food centre. ⸻ 1. Old Airport Road Fried Hokkien Mee (#01-99) ★★★★☆ (4/5) A wet-style Hokkien Mee with noticeable wok hei. While the prawn flavour is relatively mild, the $8 portion is generous, featuring four prawns along with pork and sotong. A satisfying plate and good value for those who enjoy a slightly soupy version. ⸻ 2. Famous Old Airport Fried Oyster (#01-101) ★★★☆☆ (3/5) Tried the $10 3-in-1 oyster omelette with oysters, prawns, and squid. Portion was generous, but the omelette was soft and soggy, heavy on tapioca flour, and lacked crispness. Prawns were overcooked, and squid ran out quickly. Not worth the price. ⸻ 3. Chong Pang Huat BBQ (#01-90) ★★★☆☆ (3/5) Prices are higher than typical hawker stalls, with $1.60 chicken wings and small satay portions. Value was disappointing, and hygiene concerns left a poor impression. Unlikely to return. ⸻ 4. Jin Fried Rice (#01-63) ★★★★★ (5/5) One of the best fried rice stalls I’ve tried. The mala fried rice with Chinese sausage, sunny-side-up egg, and pork chop was fragrant and full of flavour. Despite switching from Japanese rice to regular rice, the quality remains excellent. The pork chop was juicy and a clear standout. A must-try. ⸻ 5. Chuan Loo Bee Hokkien Food (#01-111) ★★☆☆☆ (2/5) The only stall open after 10pm, so I ordered the Imperial Pork Ribs Rice. Despite being cooked to order, the pork was extremely tough, and the sauce tasted odd and unpleasant. Very disappointing and not worth the price. ⸻ 6. Whampoa Soya Bean (#01-68) ★★★★☆ (4/5) Offers more than just soya beancurd and drinks, with a good variety of traditional desserts. While cold soya drinks can be slightly diluted, the desserts are excellent. Recommended: Soya beancurd with ginkgo & lotus nuts, peach gum soup, taro peach gum soup, yam ball soya milk. ⸻ 7. Unkai Japanese Cuisine (#01-88) ★★★★★ (5/5) A great variety of bentos and set meals at wallet-friendly prices. The salmon bowl came with a generous piece of salmon on fluffy Japanese rice. Simple, satisfying, and good value. Will return to try more items. ⸻ 8. Western Barbeque (#01-53) ★★★☆☆ (3/5) Despite the long queues, the chicken chop didn’t stand out. No bun is provided, and the only sauce available was garlic sauce, which lacked flavour. Decent, but there are better western options nearby. ⸻ 9. Famous Kallang Airport Fried Oyster (#01-55) ★★☆☆☆ (2/5) Generous with oysters, but the omelette was overly oily. The excess oil overshadowed the dish. Still searching for a better fried oyster omelette. ⸻ 10. Salt (#01-128) ★★★★☆ (4/5) A western-style stall selling spaghetti, chicken chop, herbal chicken, and fried wings. I tried the Sous Vide Grilled Chicken with Aglio Olio. The aglio olio was decent, garlicky, and not too oily. The chicken chop was glazed with teriyaki sauce instead of the usual western sauces. While acceptable, $9.90 feels expensive for a hawker centre given the portion and simplicity.

Review:
This place has countless options for food so there will be something for everyone; from barbeque chicken wings, desserts such as egg tarts, western food (mostly Hainanese), Chinese food (fried rice, soup dumplings, etc.), to Muslim food varieties. The portion size can vary according to which store you order from, as there are multiple stores that sell similar food items, and some with slightly different recipes which can change the texture and the taste profile. As with all hawker centres, you will have to clear your tables and place the trays in the designated tray return area. It will definitely be noisy around the center area but there are seats where it's a little quieter in the edge spots if you want to have a quieter experience. Expect the place to be crowded during lunch and dinner so finding a table can be difficult during these peak periods. You may have to share a table with others, so be polite and ask if they can share their table if you cannot find one. Otherwise, you can take your time to look for a seat while you wait for your food or come by during less crowded periods after 8pm or before 6pm. I went to this place around 7-8pm but I still managed to find a seat. Most of the stalls will give you a buzzer when you order so you can keep track of when your food is ready.

Kitty and I were on the lookout for a lunch spot and turned to Google to find Lei Cha options, which led us to a highly-rated Lei Cha restaurant in the Geylang area. Our experience at this establishment was a mix of satisfaction and room for improvement. The Lei Cha dish, though flavorful, lacked the ideal temperature, not reaching the comforting warmth that would enhance its overall enjoyment. Additionally, the soup, while tasty, was a bit dilute, missing the robustness expected in traditional Lei Cha. The service at the restaurant was commendable, with attentive staff creating a pleasant dining atmosphere. The presence of free-flow peanuts for self-service was a nice touch, adding to the welcoming ambiance. Pricing was reasonable, with white Lei Cha rice at four dollars fifty cents and brown rice at five dollars, a justifiable value. During our meal, Kitty noted her preference for the Lei Cha served in the Punggol area. While the taste of the soup was similar at both places, she found that the soup at the reviewed establishment was slightly dilute in comparison. Nevertheless, she expressed a continual preference for the Lei Cha experience in one Punggol hawker centre. The stall owner recommended their 客家南乳炸肉 (Hakka Fried Pork), which Kitty found to be very nice. If you visit this place, consider ordering this dish to enhance your dining experience. Taking all aspects into account, including feedback on the dilute soup and rice temperature, we awarded the Geylang Lei Cha establishment a four-star rating. Our culinary journey highlighted areas of improvement for an even more enjoyable dining experience.

restaurant: Thunderbolt Tea by Boon Lay Traditional Hakka Lui Cha

Review:
Goodyear Seafood Village Tampines offers a lovely destination for family and friend gatherings in a laid back kampong style setting. The restaurant’s Pontian style herbal bak kut teh, served in a claypot, is fragrant and flavourful with a herbal depth that’s lighter than Teochew versions but balanced with garlic and ginseng. The ribs are firm yet tender and absorb the broth beautifully, making it a satisfying shared dish. Aside from bak kut teh, the zi char menu shines. The Assam fish head is a standout with a tangy spicy sauce made from scratch that delivers a satisfying depth. It showcases fresh sea bass served with vegetables and pineapple. Other highlights include golden garlic pork, prawn paste chicken, cabbage chicken claypot, hotplate tofu and salted egg yolk pork ribs. Portions are generous and flavours bold enough for sharing. The ambience is rustic and peaceful. Dining here feels like stepping into a Malaysian kampong with open air seating and greenery around. The venue is spacious with both indoor and outdoor seating options, making it family friendly. Service is casual and warm though not highly polished. Staff are generally friendly. Parking can be a challenge on weekends and reservations are wise if dining in larger groups. Delivery and takeaway through WhatsApp is also available if you prefer to enjoy the food at home. Overall experience offers great value. Expect to spend around 8 to 13 dollars per bowl for bak kut teh, with zi char mains starting from 12 dollars depending on size. The generous portions, rich herbal broth, and standout dishes like Assam fish head and prawn paste chicken make it worth the slight effort to travel out a bit. For family or friend gatherings this is a solid choice with delicious dishes suited to sharing, affordable pricing, relaxed vibe, and a touch of rustic charm you don’t often find in the city.

restaurant: GoodYear Seafood Village Tampines (Zi Char and Bak Kut Teh)

Review:
This hawker centre is pretty airy. To avoid the crowd and queue, best to come before 8am, both weekdays and weekends. If you are a wanton mee lover, wouldn't want you to miss this - Xing Ji wanton noodle! Its mee gia served is springy (al-dente), veg given is always fresh (unlike many wanton stalls that sell "old" caixin that is "too fibrous" to swallow) & wanton size is just nice - bite-sized. Paired up with its boss' homemade chilli, it's simply heaven! It's usually sold out fast (esp Mon, before 11am) on weekdays.Closed on Tue & Wed. Next must-try: Thosai, Appam @ Rajarani Thosai. Another long queue if you come after 8am.. every thosai is served fresh n piping hot. It's no wonder its queue never stops (unless sold out, oc) For nice aromatic local nanyang kopi, go for Quan Fang. $1.40 for Kopi - ask for di lo siew dai (di lo: direct down; siew dai: less sweet) - then u can savour the pure goodness of the kopi with condensed milk added. Ask for Kopi-O, if u just wanna enjoy a cuppa coffee with only sugar. No sugar option? Ask for: Kopi-O Kosong Xiong Kee fried carrot cake (2 stalls - one operated by a couple, the other operated by their son) is another go-to if you enjoy a savoury plate of fried black or white carrot cake. Both stalls are yummylicious. The other carrot cake stall on the other side of the market is pretty good too, offering tumeric option. For glutinous rice lovers, can try the stall located right behind the Tiong Bahru fried fish ball, Yi Le Shu Shi. Oh ya.. the Chai Chee Pork porridge is for you, if you fancy thick savoury bowl of porridge, cooked to perfection. Each portion is of reasonable size, so if you have a smaller stomach space, best to come with a few friends so you can try all the different stalls. If not, just make a few more trips!

Review:
Each year during Ramadan I make it a tradition to first bring the family and then my non-Muslim extended family of kakis to the festive bazaars. Bazaar...for Ramadan. Not a repurposed pasar malam. Where I grew up anticipating and looking forward to festive traditional offerings — especially soulfood that will break my resistance or restrain....for health reasons.....that I'll be damned over — and not the proliferation of supposedly creative fusion which often are the hipster young fascination with Western cuisines which they sadly not only butcher at times but rehash for localised taste. At times using cheaper pseudo ingredients and slathering with overly hot toppings to mask the mediocre passable copies. Anyway I hardly fancy those. What I want to lament is the glaring absence — if any it is scattered and few — of traditional Ramadan or Raya soulfood favourites that I don't see many talk or raise about. It can't just be me. If I am blunt I'll say what used to be a great festive family affair at a beautiful bazaar, where we visit to soak in the vibe and sample the offerings, has been robbed and hijacked by 'vendors' who can afford the high rent who in turn sell high and expensive. Terrible. Where we no longer or hardly see committed makciks or pakciks lovingly peddle what they offer just for Ramadan and for some to do so to sadaqah. What a sad state. The worst is this year's supposedly largest — not .....with plenty of empty spaces obviously untaken — Geylang Ramadan Bazaar. It is a pathetic disguised tourist-bait glorified pasar malam. If you want classic traditional food that won't cost an arm and leg then for Geylang area head over to the food centre above the market. No hipster gimmick in sight. Just good ole familiar mouth-baiting classic Malay or nusantara food. And festive drinks that are traditional and not charged at inflated cafe prices. One wonders if the ones who planned all these factor in consideration for heart and soul. For respect and love for our culture. Yes, I'm naive and hopeful. Profit is sadly evident in play.

Output:
restaurant: Geylang Serai Market and Food Centre

Seng Kee Black Chicken Herbal Soup is a solid go-to spot for late-night zi char, especially if you’re craving something hearty and comforting after hours. Located along Changi Road, it’s well known for staying open late, making it a popular supper destination for night owls and shift workers alike. The food here leans towards classic, no-frills zi char done well. The chao ta bee hoon is a standout, with good wok hei and generous ingredients that make it satisfying without being overly greasy. The fried pork with fermented beancurd was also really average for me and not super unique. Still, most dishes are well executed and comforting, especially when enjoyed fresh and hot. Overall, Seng Kee delivers reliable zi char with a strong supper appeal. It may not be the cheapest option around, but if you’re looking for a filling, late-night meal with familiar flavours and decent portions, it’s a dependable choice worth returning to.

Review:
Ponggol Nasi Lemak Centre sits tucked in the everyday hustle—unassuming frontage, open windows, and the comforting aroma of coconut rice, sambal, and fried goodies welcoming you in. Inside, it’s a blend of hawker energy and family rhythm: metal tables, plastic stools, lunch crowds, and the occasional diner asking in Malay for extra ikan bilis. They do what they do with no frills but serious care. The nasi lemak arrives with fluffy, fragrant rice, each grain carrying creaminess but not sogginess. The sambal has a measured heat—not numbing or flat but soulful, slightly sweet with a hint of smokiness, picking up complexity at the edges. You’ll find crispy fried chicken with skin that snaps under your fork, ikan bilis that crunch, peanuts toasted, and custard egg just soft enough to ooze without chaos. What stands out is how the flavours balance—nothing overpowers. The sambal, the rice, the sides—they hold their own but also support each other. It’s not gimmicky; it’s the kind of plate you taste room-by-room, noticing little things you’ll want again. Service is hawker speed but with care. The workers are efficient without being robotic—tea top-ups come without asking, and they’ll clear tonight’s empty plates to make space for more. Prices stay kind, making this place as satisfying for daily habit as for those occasional cravings. If you’re around Punggol or passing through and want a solid plate of nasi lemak that hits both heart and hunger, this is one you’ll keep coming back to.

Review:
Tucked away in two modest shop houses along the ever-buzzing Geylang stretch, JB Ah Meng doesn't look like much from the outside-but come evening, it's packed to the brim with hungry diners who know exactly what they're here for. This zi char joint has built a loyal following, thanks to its menu of over 30 classic Johor Bahru-style dishes. If you're familiar with Malaysian style zi char, you'll likely spot your favourites right away. And while some dishes hit the mark more than others, there are a few standouts worth mentioning. The famed JB San Lou Beehoon came out as expected-pressed flat and crisped up on both sides, delivering that signature wok hei. Prawn rolls were decent but unmemorable. A surprising highlight was the fried spicy lala, which packed a punch and had us reaching for more. In short, JB Ah Meng makes a strong case for those craving a zi char fix without making the trip across the Causeway. It's not quite a JB clone, but for a night out in Singapore with friends over comforting, wok-kissed dishes-it's a worthy contender.

Around us, the sound of clinking beer bottles and chatter made the food even better. Circuit Road isn’t just a hawker centre — it’s a flavour-packed escape.

Review:
Donkey and I are obsessed with prawns, so we'd been wanting to try Zhup Zhup by One Prawn & Co for ages, especially since it has a Michelin Bib Gourmand! We finally got a chance to go when we were on our way to the Garmin service center. I had Zhup Zhup by One Prawn & Co saved on our Google Map for a long time. When we got there, we saw they had a pretty big menu, and a lot of people were ordering the clay pot dishes. It's in a coffee shop, but they had a good variety of food, as you can see in the photos Donkey uploaded. The liver roll was amazing! It was super savory and used pork liver instead of the usual stuff. The owner said we'd like it if we liked pork liver. I don't normally like liver, but even I tried it and thought it was good! There was no weird smell at all, and I actually enjoyed it. The crispy prawn crackers didn't have that oily taste, either. They were clean and tasted great. For our main dish, we got the claypot prawn noodles, which seemed to be really popular. They had both dry and wet versions, and we went with the wet one. I was surprised that they put the clams, pork ribs, and prawns in their own claypot instead of cooking everything together. The claypot definitely added to the flavor of the whole dish. If we had known that, we would have order the dry version instead. The Hokkien Mee also came in a claypot, and it tasted so unique. I can't really describe it, but it was different from any Hokkien Mee I've had before. The owner recommended the Hibiscus Orange drink, and it came in a teapot with two glasses. But it was only lukewarm, and by the time we were halfway through our meal, it was practically cold. That's definitely something they could improve. Overall, Zhup Zhup by One Prawn & Co is a great place to eat if you like the dishes we talked about. Review:
Nestled on the bustling Banthat Thong Road, Pungdet is a charming café that has garnered a loyal following for its meticulously prepared charcoal-toasted bread. Banthat Thong Road itself has a rich history—originally known as "Phra That Thong" and once a hub for car repair shops, it has since transformed into one of Bangkok's premier culinary destinations. Today, the street is lined with a vibrant array of eateries, attracting food enthusiasts from near and far. At Pungdet, the focus is clear: delivering perfectly toasted bread with fillings that delight both the sweet and savory palate. Each piece is toasted to order over a charcoal flame, a process that takes just enough time to create a crisp, golden exterior while warming the fillings within. The result? A fragrant and irresistibly soft bite that lingers on the palate. The Offerings With an impressive selection of 22 fillings, diners are spoiled for choice. Among the highlights are: Ham and Cheese – A timeless pairing of melted cheese and smoky ham. Butter Sugar – A sweet classic with buttery richness and a delicate sprinkle of sugar. Hokkaido Milk – Smooth, creamy, and delicately sweet, inspired by Japan's famed dairy. Tuna – A savory favorite for seafood lovers. Smoked Salmon – A luxurious option with bold, smoky notes. Prices are refreshingly affordable, ranging from 20 THB for a simple butter sugar toast to 60 THB for premium fillings like smoked salmon. A Culinary Experience During my visit, I opted for the Hokkaido Milk and Thai Tea fillings. The bread, served fresh from the grill, boasted a wonderfully crisp crust and a pillowy-soft interior. The Hokkaido Milk filling was divine—creamy, light, and delicately sweet, a perfect complement to the toasted bread. The Thai Tea filling, though flavorful, leaned on the sweeter side and might be an acquired taste for some. For those seeking a savory indulgence, the Ham and Cheese filling appears to be a crowd favorite, and it’s certainly on my list for my next visit. Ambiance The café features a cozy, air-conditioned space next door, complete with tables and chairs for diners who prefer to savor their toast on-site. Fresh water and tissues are thoughtfully provided, making for a comfortable dining experience. While the buns are delightful at any time, they’re best enjoyed fresh off the grill when the textures and aromas are at their peak. Verdict Pungdet is a must-visit for anyone exploring Banthat Thong Road. Its combination of expertly toasted bread, a wide variety of fillings, and unbeatable value makes it a standout destination in Bangkok's thriving food scene. Whether you're looking for a quick snack or a leisurely treat, Pungdet delivers with charm and consistency.

Review:
I've tried Boat noodles on several occasions in Thailand and whilst I found it ok, I didn't really enjoy it all that much. Intrigued by the long queues, I tried another Thong Smith branch (CentralWorld) and loved it. This review is for my most recent visit 2 weeks ago in Siam Paragon. We went here for dinner at 6pm and there was a sizeable queue. They have a number system where you get a ticket, and your number will be displayed on a monitor (and they will call it out) when your turn is up. We probably had a 20 minute wait so it wasn't too bad. We ordered the following: Beef Boat Noodle with Ox Tongue, Beef Ball, Sliced Beef, Braised Shank and tendon. This was excellent, with the soup having a deep, rich taste. The assorted toppings were plentiful and there was also plenty of chopped vegetables in the dish. This dish is the reason to come here and it did not disappoint. Chicken Noodles with clear soup. My son chose this dish and found it very tasty. The soup was clean and refreshing, which was perfect as he was feeling a bit under the weather at the time. Nothing like Chicken Soup to make you feel better! Pork Boat Noodle without soup - Braised pork, pork ball, sliced pork. My wife chose this dish as she is not a fan of the blood contained in the soup. The dish was good, with the noodles being nice and chewy, and toppings being tasty. One thing to note is that we also ordered a little plate of Crispy pork fat, which are these wonderful bits of crunchy lard that add incredible flavourful taste to every bite you have. Highly recommended. This restaurant chain is a favourite of mine and I will make it a point to return on any subsequent visits to Thailand.

Review:
🥢 Thong Smith Siamese Boat Noodles – A Premium Twist on a Thai Classic Thong Smith offers an upscale take on traditional Thai boat noodles, known for their rich, flavorful broth and high-quality ingredients. Located in prime Bangkok malls like Siam Paragon, CentralWorld, and EmQuartier, it’s a go-to spot for locals and tourists looking to enjoy comfort food in a clean, air-conditioned setting. ✅ What’s Great • Deep, savory broth: Thick and full-bodied, especially the beef broth—intensely aromatic with hints of spices. • Premium meats: Choose from Wagyu beef, marbled pork, tenderloin, or Kurobuta. Meat is usually tender and well-cooked. • Customisable noodles: Various noodle types (rice, egg, vermicelli) and soup bases (beef or pork). • Crispy pork rinds & garlic toppings: Add satisfying crunch and aroma. • Sides like fried wontons and grilled pork neck also shine. ⚠️ What to Note • Price is higher than typical street stalls (expect around 150–300 baht per bowl). • Small portions – more suited for tasting or sharing, not for big appetites. • Some find the broth too salty, especially in the beef version. 💬 Verdict If you’re after a clean, modern setting with gourmet-quality Thai boat noodles, Thong Smith is worth a visit. While it may not have the rustic charm of a boat-side stall, it makes up for it with quality ingredients, great presentation, and reliable service.

A Fantastic Lunch at Kub Kao' Kub Pla (CentralWorld) I had a wonderful dining experience here recently. The atmosphere was great, and the food hit the mark. Here is a breakdown of what I ordered: The Standout: Crab Fried Rice 🦀 This was easily the highlight of the meal. The taste was excellent and the portion of crab meat was very generous. One thing I really appreciated was the quality of the prep—about 90% of the crab was free of fins/shells, making it very easy to enjoy. Note: The serving size is a bit small, so keep that in mind if you're extra hungry! Stir-fried Pumpkin with Salted Egg and Crab Meat 🎃 As a big fan of pumpkin, I enjoyed this dish. It was still a solid dish, but the rice definitely won the "crab ratio" contest. Tom Yum Goong 🥣 This was served piping hot, exactly how it should be. It provided a perfect "vibe shift" for my palate, offering a sharp, spicy contrast to the richer stir-fried dishes. The Finish: Longan Ice Tea 🥤 To wrap everything up, I had the Longan Ice Tea. It was refreshing, sweet, and the perfect way to end a fantastic meal. Overall Experience: Fantastic. If you're looking for high-quality Thai comfort food in CentralWorld, this is a reliable and tasty choice. Tip: If you love crab, definitely prioritize the Crab Fried Rice!

restaurant: Kub Kao' Kub Pla Central World

Review:
🌟 Comfort Thai Food with Hits and Misses – A Realistic Take on Kub Kao’ Kub Pla (CentralWorld) We stopped by Kub Kao’ Kub Pla at CentralWorld for lunch, and while the experience had a few bumps, it still offered some memorable highlights. The star of the meal was definitely the Southern Thai Crab Curry with Butterfly Pea Vermicelli. The crab meat was tender and fresh, and the southern-style curry packed a rich, spicy punch. Pouring the curry over the vibrant butterfly pea vermicelli gave each bite a delightful blend of heat and floral aroma — beautifully balanced and visually striking. We also had the Stir-Fried Chinese Kai Lan with Crispy Pork, a classic dish we usually enjoy. The pork was nicely crisped, but we found the overall flavour a bit flat. It lacked the salty umami kick from the salted fish paste — the chef had added too little, which was disappointing given how much it could have elevated the dish. Lastly, we had the Deep-Fried Seabass with Fish Sauce, although it arrived late due to a forgotten order by the waitress. While the fish itself was fresh and well-cooked, it was heavily salted, which made it overly intense. It came with a separate side of shredded green mango, red onions, and fish sauce — very tangy and sharp, almost overwhelming. We wished we had gone with the grilled or steamed version instead. Service felt rushed due to the crowd, and though the staff were polite, we were slightly let down by the missed order and the lack of any gesture to smooth over the delay — even something small like a complimentary dessert or ice cream would’ve gone a long way. ⸻ ✨ Overall: A lively, stylish spot with good food and beautiful presentation, but our experience didn’t feel as polished as expected. Still, that crab curry vermicelli? Worth returning for.

Output:
restaurant: Kub Kao' Kub Pla Central World

Review:
Kub Kao’ Kub Pla is a must try for all Thai cuisine fans. We passed this restaurant several times and every day we saw a long queue of people seated outside the restaurant. So the best time to come is around 11am when they just open so that you will be seated rather than wait for a table. Dishes ordered for lunch were : Deep Fried Baby Shrimps with Betel Leaves (Starter), Spicy Papaya Salad with Salted Egg, Stir Fried Melinjo Leaves with Eggs and Crab Meat Omelette. The Deep Fried Baby Shrimp is very flavourful, crispy bite sized shrimp morsels, fried to perfection and seasoned with herbs and spices. The inside is tender and succulent and it comes with a sweet and spicy peanut and cucumber sauce. The Papaya Sauce is a dish here that is not comparable to the Thai Papaya Salads in Singapore or Malaysia. This is the authentic Thai style where the papaya and ingredients are fresh and every bite is crunchy and refreshing. The tiny shrimps are tasty and crispy that you can eat the shells too. The salted egg gives it a nice ‘lift’. We enjoyed the simple yet flavourful Melinjo leaves stir fried with garlic. The slightly bitter taste blended well with the savoury eggs. The best dish on the table was the Crab Meat Omelette. Fluffy and tender filled with lumps of succulent crab meat. The sweetness of the crab meat complemented the wrapped fluffy yet crispy egg omelette. Never in my life have I eaten so much crab meat at one sitting ! The crab meat omelette was served with a sweet and sour sauce that enhances its taste. For dessert we had their Taro Pearls in sweet coconut milk which was served warm and had yam pearls, yam cubes and slices of coconut . The fresh mango & sticky rice, a truly Thai classic did not fail to please our taste buds. We will return to try the other offerings in their menu.

Output:
restaurant: Kub Kao' Kub Pla Central World

In such a prestigious location and with a Michelin label, diners deserve more than just branding. This experience felt like a cash grab hiding behind a name that no longer represents the quality it promises — at least not at this branch. ⸻ ⚠️ Bottom Line: Michelin status should not be used lightly — and certainly not as a marketing tool when the food doesn’t uphold its name. Their specialty is the traditional Thai snack "Khanom Krok," a bite-sized dessert made with coconut milk, rice flour, and flour, similar to takoyaki. Last weekend, I had the absolute pleasure of dining at Kaitainam, a Thai restaurant that’s quickly become my new favorite spot. Tucked away in a cozy corner of town, Kaitainam offers an inviting atmosphere with warm lighting, subtle Thai decor, and a soft hum of chatter that makes you feel right at home. From the moment I walked in, the staff greeted me with genuine smiles and a level of hospitality that’s hard to come by these days. The menu is a delightful journey through Thailand’s culinary landscape, and I started with their papaya salad—som tam—which was a revelation. I couldn’t resist trying their mango sticky rice for dessert, and it was the ultimate finale—sweet, ripe mango paired with sticky rice drizzled in coconut cream that melted in my mouth. What sets Kaitainam apart is the attention to detail. Every dish felt fresh, vibrant, and made with care, like it was crafted just for me. The service was impeccable—attentive without being overbearing—and the prices were surprisingly reasonable for the quality. Whether you’re a Thai food aficionado or just dipping your toes in, Kaitainam delivers an experience that’s as authentic as it is unforgettable. I’m already counting the days until my next visit!

Review:
Visited Cook Chai Dim Sum during my trip to Hatyai and it was truly one of the highlights when it comes to local breakfast experiences. This spot is very popular, not only among tourists but also locals, which already tells you a lot about its reputation. If you are visiting Hatyai, this place is often mentioned as a must-try breakfast stop, and after dining here, I can see why. The staff are friendly and attentive, despite the busyness of the restaurant. Even when the place was quite packed, the service still felt smooth and efficient, which is impressive considering the constant flow of customers. The environment is lively and bustling, and while it can feel a little crowded at times, it is still comfortable enough for dining. In fact, the busy atmosphere adds to the charm of the place, giving you a sense of the local dining culture in Hatyai. When it comes to food, there are a lot of varieties to choose from. The selection of dim sum is wide, ranging from steamed buns, dumplings, siu mai, har gao, and many other small plates that are fun to try and share. The food taste is decent—nothing overly fancy, but tasty and satisfying, especially for a casual breakfast. The food portion matches the price, so you get good value for what you pay. The pricing is reasonable, which makes it easy to try a little bit of everything without worrying too much about the bill. What makes this place even more special is that other than dim sum, you can also order bak kut teh. Having a hot clay pot of herbal soup alongside a spread of dim sum gives you a hearty and unique breakfast combination that you don’t often find elsewhere. It’s definitely worth trying if you want to experience something beyond the usual dim sum. Overall, I would say Cook Chai Dim Sum is an essential stop if you’re in Hatyai. It combines good food, fair prices, and an authentic local experience. The mix of locals and tourists dining together makes the atmosphere unique, and it gives you the feeling that you’re eating where everyone in town comes for breakfast. Definitely worth visiting at least once during your stay.

Review:
CookChai Dimsum is a lively and authentic dim sum restaurant that captures both the heart and flavor of Southern Thailand’s food culture. From the moment you walk in, the atmosphere feels warm and bustling, with families, friends, and locals enjoying their meals together in a casual setting. The interior is simple yet full of character, decorated with traditional photos, bright signs, and the unmistakable aroma of freshly steamed dim sum. The highlight here is, of course, the dim sum itself. Steaming bamboo baskets filled with classic selections such as siu mai and har gow arrive hot and flavorful, with generous fillings and a satisfying texture. Beyond dim sum, the restaurant offers impressive hot dishes. The herbal pork soup served in a clay pot is rich, aromatic, and deeply comforting, blending Chinese herbs with tender meat and mushrooms. Another standout is the sizzling hot plate dish packed with minced pork, mushrooms, and chilies, which delivers both spice and bold flavor. Pairing this with the crispy golden egg omelet creates a balance of textures that complements the meal perfectly. Service is friendly and efficient, even with the busy crowd, and prices are very reasonable for the generous portions. Overall, CookChai Dimsum is not just a place to eat but an experience that celebrates traditional Chinese-Thai flavors. It’s highly recommended for anyone looking for a hearty breakfast or brunch in the area.

Review:
It’s breakfast time, we’re hungry, and let’s face it we need to eat. But that doesn’t mean we’ve lost all standards. Now, we’re not being snobs here… just practical. Dim sum in Thailand? Really? That’s like flying to Italy and ordering sushi. Sure, it exists but should you? It’s not indigenous, it’s not iconic, and it’s definitely not what Thai kitchens wake up thinking about at dawn. We’re in the land of tom yum and mango sticky rice. So, while dim sum might be available, it’s a no-brainer to stay away. Why settle for lukewarm siew mai pretending to be Cantonese when there’s a steaming bowl of boat noodles waiting to give you a hug? Some might say we’re being picky. Nah — we’re just making smart choices with our stomachs. After all, breakfast is too important to waste on mediocrity.

Review:
If you’re visiting Hatyai, Chokdee Dim Sum is definitely one of those breakfast spots that locals and tourists alike recommend, so I decided to give it a try. It was a good experience overall, and I can see why it’s so popular. The staff here are friendly and attentive, even though the place was quite busy during breakfast hours. Service was quick, and they patiently guided me through the dim sum selection process, which is a nice touch if it’s your first time there. There are two dining areas – the main store and a newer, more spacious dining area just opposite. I chose to sit in the main store, as it is closer to the dim sum counter and has a more authentic, bustling atmosphere. Taste-wise, the dim sum itself was decent – I would say it was just ordinary compared to other places I have tried, but still enjoyable. I also ordered their Bah Kut Teh, which was slightly salty for my liking, though taste can be very subjective and others might find it just right. Overall, Chokdee Dim Sum is a nice breakfast experience if you are in Hatyai. The variety of dishes, reasonable pricing, and lively atmosphere make it worth a visit. Just be sure to go early, as the place can get really crowded during peak hours.

The restaurant offers a wide variety of dishes — both Thai and Western options like pizza and sandwiches — plus a great selection of beers. In total, we paid only 530 Baht for everything, which is incredibly affordable for such a touristy area. At the end, they even gave us a small mint candy with the bill — a nice touch. Overall, a great experience and definitely a place we’d recommend to anyone visiting the area.

Thai basil lifts it with an herbaceous perfume, cauliflower and dense mushrooms give chew and bounce, while slices of crusty yet fluffy baguette beg to be dragged through every last drop.
