How they achieve such delicious meatballs without meat is beyond me, when such convincing golden-crumbed spheres deliver a fragrant crunch, giving way to a moist legume filling that mimics ground meat. The fermented soybean sauce layers on a funky depth, and the mango salads bring a fruity spark. Finally, it's decorated with a glint of edible gold leaf and a fog of dry ice to drive the spectacle.

Considering the District 1 location, portion, and packaging, I think the price is reasonable. Overall, it’s a very good bánh mì experience. Definitely worth trying if you’re nearby! 🍞🌿🥒

I chose Cam Thi when a foreign friend wanted to eat Vietnamese food because it has three things: 1. A true hidden gem of Saigon: I've always believed that how a restaurant "hides" itself is also part of the story. Cam Thi didn't choose the bustling facade of Ho Hao Hon Street. They chose a side alley off Alley 53. This isn't a coincidence; it's a deliberate experiential "architecture." You step into the small alley, and an old wooden house appears, a door completely separating you from the outside world. 2. A culture of "contact" through a shared meal: Instead of ordering individual dishes, we ordered a home-style meal. This is the most valuable "culture." We shared braised meat, picked from the same plate of stir-fried vegetables, sipped from the same bowl of crab and water spinach soup, and shared clams and rice crackers… 3. The space, the story, and the food are all meticulously prepared. I rank Cam Thi in the mid-range nostalgic segment. The price is very reasonable for an excellent experience right in District 1. It's more upscale than a typical casual eatery, but warmer and more intimate than fine dining at other famous restaurants they've visited. After the meal, my friend said, "This is not just a meal, this is a story." Cons: Very crowded during peak hours; people are wearing traditional Vietnamese long dresses and headscarves and taking tons of photos. If you want a quieter atmosphere, choose a time after 1:30 PM.

The Hungry Pig: Where Bui Vien’s Chaos Meets a Culinary Twist Tucked away in the labyrinthine alleys behind the ever-buzzing Bui Vien Walking Street, The Hungry Pig isn’t a café you stumble upon — it’s one you discover. Hidden behind the raucous hum of backpacker bars and street music, this unassuming spot has earned a reputation that quietly travels through word of mouth. This café isn’t chasing authenticity in the traditional sense. Instead, it delights in reinvention — a playful collision of East and West. Think King Kong meets Godzilla, but on a plate. The result is familiar comfort food with an unexpected Asian edge — bold, inventive, and surprisingly harmonious. The menu reads like a witty conversation between culinary cultures. Forget about finding your standard Bodega Sandwich or Molesey Beef-Dripped Chippy. Here, the creativity lies not just in the recipes but in the names themselves — clever, tongue-in-cheek, and impossible to resist. Here’s what stood out during my visit: All Day English Breakfast – crafted by someone who truly understands that the way to a man’s heart is undeniably through his stomach. Fish & Chips – a nostalgic nod to home, though I found myself longing for those traditional beef drippings (curse you, healthy living!). Hamlette — bitten by the Bard, yet a charlatan in the written arts; but, I dare say, a master in the divine art of cookery. Pig Lebowski – hearty, unapologetic, and undoubtedly made by Dudes for Dudes. Notorious P.I.G. – because some dishes don’t just speak; they declare. Each plate carried that satisfying blend of humour and heart — a café that doesn’t take itself too seriously yet delivers on every bite. So, next time you’re wandering through the chaotic charm of Bui Vien, take a detour down its quieter corners. There you’ll find The Hungry Pig — a tiny nook where fusion finds its fun, and brekkies might just last all day.....Cheers!

Review:
I ordered the C2 hot-stone beef pho, which comes with raw beef slices and cooked beef brisket. On the side you get beef broth, scallions, bean sprouts, lemongrass, Thai basil, and fresh chili. The taste is very close to the classic pho I’ve had before. The stone bowl arrives piping hot, so you can cook the raw beef yourself, almost like a mini hot pot. Review:
Most people can’t even decide on a tie, and here they are handing you two menus and expecting you to behave. It’s an embarrassment of riches, really—Mặn Mòi and Hum Lounge playing house in a garden that’s far more tranquil than my last three massages. Here is how you handle a table for three without looking like an amateur: The Nem Vuông Nấm: These mushroom squares are a miracle of engineering. Usually, "plant-based" is just a polite way of saying "we ran out of ideas," but these are crispy, golden little boxes of secrets. They have more personality than most people I've worked with. The "Wrapped Meat" Ritual: Whether it’s the Gà nướng lá dứa (Pandan Chicken) or the Bò nướng ống tre (Beef in Bamboo), it’s dinner as a DIY project. You wrap the meat, you commit to the flavor, and you pretend you’ve done something productive with your hands. It’s smoky, tender, and—since we’re skipping the pork—tactically brilliant. The Cơm Chiên Gà Đồng, Lá É: Fried rice with lemon basil. It smells better than a French perfume and actually delivers on the promise. It’s the kind of starch that doesn't just sit there; it performs. The Dừa Nướng: They grill the coconut because, apparently, just being a fruit wasn’t dramatic enough. It’s chilled, it’s sweet, and it’s the only thing in this humidity that actually works as advertised. The Verdict: We skipped the pork and I didn't feel a hint of deprivation. Sit in the garden, order with the confidence of a man with a gold card, and let everyone think you’re a genius. It’s much easier than actually being one.

restaurant: Mặn Mòi, Tao Đàn - 34 Võ Văn Tần

As of today, my father is still experiencing a low-grade fever. I want to keep this review as objective as possible. The restaurant itself is beautifully designed, and the shop on the first floor is charming—we spent around $450 there buying a lot of crafts. The food was good, though given the reputation and hype, we were expecting more. Notably, the only member of our family who did not become ill was my mother. The only dish she did not eat was the crab hot pot. When the hot pot was brought to our table, it was not boiling. After waiting for some time, we asked the waitress for assistance three separate times. The first time, we were told to wait a few more minutes. The second time, we were told that the soup had already been boiled in the kitchen and was safe to eat. Coming from another Asian country, my understanding is that hot pot should remain actively boiling while cooking raw ingredients to ensure food safety. We were reassured that this was the traditional way to eat it and that it would be fine. Eventually, the staff portioned the soup and cooked the meat and vegetables for us in the pot, which was still not boiling. Trusting their guidance, we ate the dish. My mother chose not to eat anything from the hot pot, and she was the only one who did not fall ill. I cannot say with certainty what specific pathogen caused our illness. However, three out of four people becoming seriously sick within hours of the same meal is deeply concerning. While local diners may be accustomed to certain practices, a restaurant of this caliber—especially one frequented by international guests—should take extra care with food safety and preparation standards. This was an extremely painful and costly experience for my family, and I hope this feedback is taken seriously!!!

Review:
The other more famous shop has more queues over Bánh Mì Hồng Hoa, and is generally the popular spot for tourists, but don’t let fool you. Bánh Mì Hồng Hoa is far superior (atleast for me) and here is why: 1. Size: Bigger isn’t always better. 🙈 The competitor offers just one massive size of banh mi while Hong Hoa gives you an option; one that is as big as the rival shop and one that is just the right size that’ll give you the perfect bite with everything in it (bread, veggies, and meat). Since the competitor’s is so big, it’s impossible to get that perfect bite, unless of course, you have an equally as massive mouth. Lol. 2. Variety: The other shop has only one Banh Mi option which is the traditional “put every Vietnamese charcuterie” in a baguette. It’s tasty and the most traditional but you’d get tired of it easily. More options would be better. Meanwhile, Hong Hoa has 6 varieties to choose from with their Bread with Roast Pork option being the best! 3. Price: The other shop’s pricing, as mentioned by many, is too expensive at 73K VND. Yes, it is big. But Hong Hoa offers the same size at just 55K VND. 🤷🏻‍♀️ 4. Taste: Not gonna lie, the rival’s is delicious as heck but there is a thing as over filling. It has too much meat, butter, and paté that it has become too overwhelming on the taste buds. They give you separate packs of fresh greens and pickled vegetables but even that isn’t enough to balance out the flavors. On the other hand, Hong Hoa’s is perfectly balanced. We tried both their Roast Pork and Mixed Meat one which is similar to Huynh Hoa’s to give it a fair comparison. For the Mixed Meat one, the slices of ham and paté taste better here although not as generous and the other shop. Again, Quality > Quantity. 😉 And for the Roast Pork one, it is hands down the best Banh Mi I’ve had in my life!!!!! The pork is nicely charred and its fattines goes really well with the pickled veggies. It meat is kinda reminiscent of Pork Sisig (a Filipino dish). It even has that spicy little kick from the chilies. It’s a sandwich worth the trip back to Saigon! 💯 Either way, both these Saigon banh mi shops made the most famous stall (for tourists) in Hanoi, Banh Mi 25, taste like utter crap. Lol. 🤣

The toppings are genuinely good, and as someone who really loves com tam and has tried many places, I can see why Ba Ghiền is so well known. That said, I think the experience is best when you customize it a bit to suit your own taste. Personally, I find the grilled chicken juicier and less dry than the pork chop. The rice is on the drier side and clearly meant to be eaten with soup. Since I usually skip the soup, I add a little water and microwave the rice when eating at home, to make it softer. One small tip is to order outside peak hours, either before or after lunch or dinner, as the food tends to be prepared more carefully. For example, when I ordered around 9 am and asked for extra chili, they were very generous.

Review:
I visited a long-established Cơm Tấm restaurant in Ho Chi Minh City for the first time. The restaurant is featured in the Michelin guide, so I went there with high expectations. The restaurant had a spacious area with about 40 seats, but it was very crowded even when I visited around 1:30 PM. You can order in Vietnamese, a little English, and by pointing and using gestures. There are only six basic set menus, so it's easy to order. The food arrived in two minutes after I ordered. It's very speedy. The taste of the Cơm Tấm was characterized by its sweet sauce. The pork was very large and quite substantial, which might be too much for some women. The restaurant lacks a sense of cleanliness in appearance. During busy times, it's common to find trash on the floor, and there's a slight smell of food waste. Some customers were smoking while walking. However, this is a common sight in long-established local restaurants, so if you've visited Vietnam several times, it shouldn't be a problem. Japanese people visiting for the first time might experience a bit of culture shock. If you want to eat a lot of Cơm Tấm cheaply, I think Cơm Tấm enthusiasts will find it worth repeating!

Review:
I've been here twice, and overall, it’s been a great dining experience. All the pizzas are made to order, and it takes about 15 to 20 minutes for them to be served after placing your order. Watching the guys working busily at the oven adds to the whole vibe. The freshness of the food is pretty good. The squid ink rice is tender and comes with a skewer of springy squid meat, which is quite nice. For pizzas, you can order half-and-half. I recommend the Burrata Parma Ham flavor—the parma ham adds a savory taste, while the creamy cheese brings a rich texture, all on a crispy thin crust. The combination of flavors and textures is very satisfying. The cheese pizza is also good. The table comes with honey, which you can drizzle on top. Two slices of pizza are enough to leave you feeling content. The tuna salad is fresh and tasty, though the portion is a bit small. For drinks, they serve beer with meals, about 250ml per glass. I wouldn’t recommend the Da Lat Whey Stout—it lacks the rich, bold taste of a stout. The honey wine beer, on the other hand, is great—it’s quite sweet and very drinkable. The only issue is that there’s often a queue. If you don’t make a reservation in advance, you might have to wait even after arriving. I once saw someone come at 2 p.m., only to be told they could only get a table at 4 p.m. They left looking disappointed, and I’m not sure if they ever came back. Alternatively, you could ride a motorbike here and, if there’s a wait, take a stroll to the nearby Pink Church or the My Son Sculpture Museum, which are just a few hundred meters away. Time will fly by before you know it. The My Son Sculpture Museum is truly amazing! But that’s another story. By the way, Ngoc provides a very good service as well.

My group of five stumbled upon this delightful Vietnamese restaurant in Ho Chi Minh City, and what a find it was. The decor immediately catches your eye, with its rich, traditional Vietnamese touches that make you feel truly immersed in the local culture. Given that we didn't have any specific recommendations from social media, we decided to be adventurous and simply order whatever caught our eye from the picture menu. To our absolute delight, every single dish was a winner not a single bad choice in the lot! A standout was the grilled pork belly. It was perfectly cooked, with a wonderfully crisp exterior that gave way to tender, juicy meat. Paired with a spicy dipping sauce, it was incredibly moreish and surprisingly light. We also thoroughly enjoyed the grilled pork with rice noodles. I’ve had this dish before in Laos, and the flavours here were just as authentic and delicious a testament to the shared culinary heritage of the region. What makes this place even better is the price. For a group of five, we were able to enjoy a fantastic, satisfying meal without breaking the bank. A brilliant spot for anyone looking for a genuine and affordable taste of Vietnam. Highly recommended!
